domains.title: Strong-Handed Man
domains.subtitle: Strength, Caves, and the Restoration of Light
domains.lead: Tajikarao is the kami of physical strength, famous for pulling Amaterasu from the cave into which she had withdrawn. His name means 'Strong-Handed Man,' and he embodies the raw power that complements the cunning of Ame-no-Uzume and the radiance of the sun goddess.

mythology.lead: Tajikarao's mythology is concentrated in the single decisive moment when he restored the sun.

myths.title: Pulling Amaterasu from the Cave
myths.text: When Amaterasu peeked out of the Ama-no-Iwato cave, drawn by Uzume's dance and her own reflection in a mirror, Tajikarao seized her hand and pulled her into the open. Some versions say he pulled the rock-door itself from its hinges. His strength overcame her withdrawal and returned light to the world.

myths.title: Aftermath
myths.text: After Amaterasu emerged, a rope called the shimenawa was stretched across the cave entrance to prevent her from withdrawing again. Tajikarao's action had made the return of order possible, but the community's rites ensured that order would endure.

myths.title: God of Strength and Caves
myths.text: Tajikarao was worshipped at caves and in places where physical strength was honored. His role as the one who breaks seals made him a patron of those who must overcome obstacles by force.

lore.syncretism: Tajikarao is a specialist deity: he does one thing, but that one thing is essential. He balances the cleverness of Uzume with brute strength, showing that cosmic restoration requires both persuasion and power. His association with caves connects him to broader Japanese beliefs about mountains as liminal spaces.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tajikarao is remembered primarily through the Amaterasu cave myth, one of Japan's most retold stories. He appears in art, drama, and popular media as the strongman who saved the world. His name is invoked when strength and decisive action are needed.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tajikarao is the strength that acts when persuasion has done its work. After Uzume made Amaterasu curious, after the mirror showed her her own light, someone had to pull. He reminds us that there are moments when only direct action will do.
lore.archaeology: Tajikarao has no major independent shrine. His significance is preserved in the cave mythology and in local cults associated with strength and mountain caves.
